text: "To Him who loved us and washed us from our sins in His own blood, and has made us kings and priests." Washed is only half the story.
explanation:
We often stop at forgiveness: He loved us and washed us. And it matters who does the washing; when Jesus washes you, your robe of righteousness shines brighter than the sun. But the sentence keeps going: "and has made us kings and priests to His God and Father."

As a priest, you come to God with worship and thanks that rise like fragrance before Him. As a king, you go out from His presence carrying His purposes, and "where the word of a king is, there is power." You're not just a forgiven sinner. You're royalty with an assignment.

text: King Uzziah tried to burn incense like a priest and was struck with leprosy. In Israel, no man could be both king and priest, except One.
explanation:
Kings ruled and priests ministered, and the two offices were kept apart. When Uzziah entered the temple to offer incense, leprosy broke out on his forehead as he argued with the priests. God was guarding a role reserved for His Son: "He shall be a priest on His throne." Melchizedek, king of Salem and priest of God Most High, was a picture of Him.

Now Jesus, the true King-Priest, has made you "a royal priesthood." What was forbidden to Israel's kings is your birthright in Christ. You worship like a priest and you reign like a king, because you're His offspring.

text: "Proclaim the praises of Him" literally means proclaim His excellencies. Your life is meant to show what He's like.
explanation:
"You are a chosen generation, a royal priesthood, a holy nation… that you may proclaim the praises of Him who called you out of darkness into His marvellous light." The word is arete: virtues, moral excellencies. It's not only songs on Sunday; it's how you do business, treat your spouse, speak to people.

Grace isn't lower than law; it aims higher. The law says, "Don't commit adultery"; grace produces a husband who loves his wife. The law says, "Don't steal"; grace makes you generous. Not because you're trying, but because you know who you are. A prince doesn't ask, "Must I?" but "May I?"

text: "Jesus, knowing that the Father had given all things into His hands… took a towel and washed the disciples' feet." Only the insecure are proud.
explanation:
In the rented upper room there was no servant to wash feet, and none of the disciples volunteered. Jesus rose from supper, laid aside His garments, wrapped a towel around Himself and knelt. But John records first what Jesus knew: that all things were in His hands, that He had come from God and was going to God.

He could stoop because He knew exactly who He was. People who are secure in their identity can afford to serve. It's insecurity that grasps for position and needs to be seen. Know that you're loved and royal in Christ, and you'll find it easy to be humble.

text: "O you of little faith" was really Jesus asking, "Why do you take so little from Me when I have so much to give?"
explanation:
Love is the hand that gives; faith is the hand that takes. When you take from people, they're depleted. When you take from God, it's as though He becomes more satisfied. That's why "without faith it is impossible to please Him."

Jesus didn't rebuke His disciples for asking too much. He gently chided them for receiving too little from a Saviour overflowing with power, provision and love. Even His corrections are beautiful. Don't be shy about taking from Him.

text: When John the Baptist doubted, Jesus didn't scold him. He said, "Go and tell John the things you hear and see."
explanation:
In prison, John sent his disciples to ask, "Are You the Coming One, or do we look for another?" Jesus let them watch Him heal, then said, "Go and tell John: the blind see, the lame walk, the lepers are cleansed, the deaf hear, the dead are raised, and the poor have the gospel preached to them. And blessed is he who is not offended because of Me."

The correction was so gentle that even the messengers didn't realise it was a correction; it was wrapped like a gift for John alone. And the cure for doubt? Hearing what Jesus has done. Tell people what He's done for you.

text: Jehoshaphat told wicked King Ahab, "I am as you are," and nearly died in Ahab's place. Be careful whom you bind yourself to.
explanation:
Jehoshaphat was a godly, blessed king of Judah. Ahab, the king of Israel who had led the nation into Baal worship, asked him to join a war that wasn't his. Jehoshaphat answered, "I am as you are, my people as your people." In battle, Ahab disguised himself while Jehoshaphat rode in royal robes, and the enemy surrounded the wrong king.

"Jehoshaphat cried out, and the Lord helped him." God's mercy rescued him, but the fight was never his. When you say "I am as you are" in marriage or in business, you share that person's fate. Choose partners worthy of who you are in Christ.
